# Erdős Problem 338, one variant: the restricted order is bounded in terms of the order

*Generated by an AI agent and machine-checked in Lean (`Erdos338.lean`); not reviewed by a human expert.*

## The theorem

A set $A$ of non-negative integers is a *basis* if, for some $h$, every large integer is a sum of at most $h$ elements of $A$, repetition allowed. The least such $h$ is its *order*. Its *restricted order* is the least $t$, if one exists, such that every large integer is a sum of at most $t$ *distinct* elements of $A$. We prove that whenever the restricted order exists, it is bounded by a number $f(h)$ that depends only on $h$, not on $A$.

This answers "yes" to question 3(ii) of Erdős and Graham (1980), formalized in Formal Conjectures as `Erdos338.erdos_338.variants.bounded_by_order`. It is a variant of Problem 338. We do not address the headline question 3(i) (which bases have a restricted order) or question 3(iii) (which bases have equal order and restricted order).

Throughout, "every large integer" means every integer from some point onward, where that threshold may depend on $A$.

**Theorem.** *There is a function $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ such that the following holds for all $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ and $h\in\mathbb N$. If*

* **(i)** *every large integer is a sum of at most $h$ elements of $A$, repetition allowed, and*
* **(ii)** *for some $t$, every large integer is a sum of at most $t$ distinct elements of $A$,*

*then every large integer is a sum of at most $f(h)$ distinct elements of $A$.*

The value of $t$ plays no role: the proof uses from (ii) only that every large integer is a sum of distinct elements of $A$.

## Idea of the proof

Call a number *$(k,q)$-robust* if it remains a sum of at most $k$ distinct elements of $A$ even after any $q$ numbers are forbidden. When $q$ is large, robust numbers can be added *with repetition*, because each copy can be represented using fresh elements. Fix any function $Q$. A counting argument shows that for every large $N$ (called a *scale*), at least $N/c$ of the numbers in $[1,2N]$ are $(2h,Q(c))$-robust, where $c$ may depend on $N$ but belongs to a finite list of constants determined by $h$ and $Q$.

A pigeonhole argument then represents every multiple of a modulus $g(c)$ between $4g(c)N$ and $10g(c)N$ as a sum of boundedly many of these robust numbers. Neither $g(c)$ nor that bound on the number of summands depends on $Q$, so we can choose $Q(c)$ large relative to both. To write a target $n$, we first adjust its residue modulo $g(c)$ using fewer than $g(c)$ distinct elements of $A$, which the robust numbers avoid. Let $c'$ be the constant at scale $N+1$. We pick $N$ so that $5g(c)N\le n<5g(c')(N+1)$. If $n>10g(c)N$, then $c'>c$, and subtracting copies of one large $(2h,Q(c'))$-robust number drops us back into the range covered at scale $N$.

## Notation and constants

Write $\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$; all intervals are intervals of integers, $|X|$ is the cardinality of $X$, and $s(G)$ is the sum of the elements of a finite set $G$ (with $s(\emptyset)=0$). All number variables below denote non-negative integers. Fix $A\subseteq\mathbb N$ and $h\ge 1$. (When $h=0$, hypothesis (i) cannot hold because $0$ is the only empty sum, so any value of $f(0)$ works.) For $r,k,q\ge 0$, let:

* $B_r$ be the set of sums of at most $r$ elements of $A$, repetition allowed, and set $b_r(N)=|B_r\cap[0,N]|$. Empty sums are allowed, so $0\in B_r$ and $B_0=\{0\}$.
* $D_{k,q}$ be the set of all $(k,q)$-robust numbers: those $n\in\mathbb N$ such that for every $W\subseteq\mathbb N$ with $|W|\le q$, there exists $G\subseteq A\setminus W$ with $|G|\le k$ and $s(G)=n$.

In particular, $D_{k,0}$ is the set of sums of at most $k$ distinct elements of $A$. Clearly $D_{k,q}\subseteq D_{k',q'}$ whenever $k\le k'$ and $q'\le q$ (monotonicity). For $c\ge 1$, define
$$g(c)=(16c^2)!,\qquad K(c)=(80c^2+2)\,g(c),\qquad Q(c)=g(c)+4h\,K(c).$$
These functions are nondecreasing in $c$. Define the sequence
$$c_0=6,\qquad c_{i+1}=3c_i\bigl(h+2c_i\,Q(c_i)\bigr),\qquad f(h)=Q(c_h).$$
Then $c_0\le c_1\le c_2\le\cdots$, and both $c_i$ and $f(h)$ depend only on $h$.

A *scale* is an integer $N\ge 1$. We say that $N$ **has type** $c$ (for $c\ge 1$) if
$$N\le c\,\bigl|D_{2h,Q(c)}\cap[1,2N]\bigr|.$$
A scale may have more than one type.

## Lemma 1 (adding robust numbers)

*(a) If $x\in D_{k,q}$ and $y\in D_{l,q+k}$, then $x+y\in D_{k+l,q}$.*

*(b) If $x_1,\dots,x_m\in D_{k,q+km}$ (not necessarily distinct), then $x_1+\dots+x_m\in D_{km,q}$.*

*Proof.* (a) Given $W\subseteq\mathbb N$ with $|W|\le q$, pick $G\subseteq A\setminus W$ with $|G|\le k$ and $s(G)=x$. Since $|W\cup G|\le q+k$, there is $H\subseteq A\setminus(W\cup G)$ with $|H|\le l$ and $s(H)=y$. Then $G$ and $H$ are disjoint subsets of $A\setminus W$, so $s(G\cup H)=x+y$ and $|G\cup H|\le k+l$.

(b) We induct on $m$. For $m=0$, take $G=\emptyset$. For $m\ge 1$, monotonicity places every $x_i$ in $D_{k,q+k(m-1)}$, so $x_1+\dots+x_{m-1}\in D_{k(m-1),q}$ by the induction hypothesis. Adding $x_m$ via part (a) (with $k(m-1)$ and $k$ in place of $k$ and $l$) completes the step. $\square$

## Lemma 2 (few numbers need a repeated summand)

*For all integers $r,N\ge 0$,*
$$b_{r+1}(N)\le\bigl|D_{r+1,0}\cap[0,N]\bigr|+r\,b_r(N).$$

*Proof.* Call a multiset of at most $r$ elements of $A$ summing to $n$ an *$r$-representation* of $n$, and call it *maximal* if no $r$-representation of $n$ contains more distinct elements. For each $w\in B_r$, fix a maximal $r$-representation $S_w$.

We claim that every $y\in B_{r+1}\setminus D_{r+1,0}$ can be written as $w+a$ with $w\in B_r$ and $a$ occurring in $S_w$. Indeed, let $M$ be a maximal $(r+1)$-representation of $y$. Because $y\notin D_{r+1,0}$, some element $a$ appears at least twice in $M$. Removing one copy of $a$ leaves an $r$-representation $M'$ of $w=y-a$ with the same distinct elements as $M$. Thus $S_w$ has at least as many distinct elements as $M$. If $a$ did not appear in $S_w$, adding $a$ to $S_w$ would give an $(r+1)$-representation of $y$ with strictly more distinct elements than $M$, contradicting the maximality of $M$.

By this claim, every $y\in (B_{r+1}\cap[0,N])\setminus D_{r+1,0}$ equals $w+a$ for some $w\in B_r\cap[0,N]$ and one of the at most $r$ distinct elements $a$ of $S_w$. There are at most $r\,b_r(N)$ such sums. $\square$

## Lemma 3 (many numbers are robust)

*Let $0\le r<h$, $N\ge 1$, $c\ge 1$, and $q\ge 0$ be integers, and set $e=b_r(N)$. If*
$$3N\le c\,b_{r+1}(N)\qquad\text{and}\qquad c\,(h+2cq)\,e\le N,$$
*then $N\le c\,\bigl|D_{2h,q}\cap[1,2N]\bigr|$.*

*Proof.* Set $X=D_{r+1,0}\cap[1,N]$ and $T=D_{2h,q}\cap[1,2N]$. For each $x\in X$, fix a set $F_x\subseteq A$ with $|F_x|\le r+1\le h$ and $s(F_x)=x$. For every $n$, define
$$P_n=\{(x,y)\in X\times X:\ x+y=n,\ F_x\cap F_y=\emptyset\}.$$

(a) *For every $u$, at most $e$ elements $x\in X$ satisfy $u\in F_x$.* For each such $x$, the number $x-u=s(F_x\setminus\{u\})$ lies in $B_r\cap[0,N]$, and the map $x\mapsto x-u$ is injective.

(b) *For every finite set $V$, at most $|V|e$ elements $x\in X$ satisfy $F_x\cap V\ne\emptyset$.* Sum (a) over $u\in V$.

(c) *If $n\notin D_{2h,q}$, then $|P_n|\le 2qe$.* Choose a set $W$ with $|W|\le q$ that meets every $G\subseteq A$ satisfying $|G|\le 2h$ and $s(G)=n$. Let $Z=\{x\in X: F_x\cap W\ne\emptyset\}$; by (b), $|Z|\le qe$. For any $(x,y)\in P_n$, the set $G=F_x\cup F_y$ has size at most $2h$ and sum $n$ (as $F_x$ and $F_y$ are disjoint), so $F_x$ or $F_y$ meets $W$. That means either $x\in Z$ or $x=n-y$ with $y\in Z$. This allows at most $2qe$ values of $x$, and $x$ determines $y=n-x$.

(d) *At most $|X|he$ pairs $(x,y)\in X\times X$ satisfy $F_x\cap F_y\ne\emptyset$.* For each $x\in X$, apply (b) with $V=F_x$.

(e) *We have $|X|^2\le |X|he+|X||T|+2N\cdot 2qe$.* Every pair in $X\times X$ either has $F_x\cap F_y\ne\emptyset$ (counted in (d)) or belongs to $P_n$ for some $n\in[1,2N]$. If $n\in T$, then $|P_n|\le |X|$ because $x$ determines $y$; if $n\notin T$, apply (c).

We now combine these bounds. Since $0\in B_r$, we have $e\ge 1$, so $|D_{r+1,0}\cap[0,N]|\le |X|+1\le |X|+e$. By Lemma 2,
$$3N\le c\,b_{r+1}(N)\le c\bigl(|X|+(r+1)e\bigr)\le c|X|+che.$$
Since $che\le c(h+2cq)e\le N$, it follows that $2N\le c|X|$, and in particular $X\ne\emptyset$. Therefore the last term in (e) is at most $2cqe|X|$. Dividing (e) by $|X|$ and multiplying by $c$ yields
$$2N\le c|X|\le c(h+2cq)e+c|T|\le N+c|T|.\qquad\square$$

## Lemma 4 (every large scale has a type)

*Assume (i). For all large $N$ there is $c\le c_h$ such that $N$ has type $c$.*

*Proof.* Choose $N_0$ so that $B_h$ contains every integer $\ge N_0$, and take $N>2N_0+c_h$. Call $r\in[0,h]$ *dense* if
$$3N\le c_{h-r}\,b_r(N).$$
Here $h$ is dense because $6\,b_h(N)\ge 6(N+1-N_0)\ge 3N$, while $0$ is not dense because $c_h\,b_0(N)=c_h<3N$. Hence there is some $r<h$ such that $r$ is not dense and $r+1$ is dense. Set $c=c_{h-r-1}$, so $c_{h-r}=3c\,(h+2c\,Q(c))$. Then $3N\le c\,b_{r+1}(N)$ and $3c\,(h+2c\,Q(c))\,b_r(N)<3N$. Applying Lemma 3 with $q=Q(c)$ shows that $N$ has type $c\le c_h$. $\square$

## Lemma 5 (sums of elements of a dense set)

*Let $N,c\ge 1$ be integers, $T\subseteq[1,2N]$ with $N\le c|T|$, and $g=g(c)$. Every multiple $n$ of $g$ satisfying $4gN\le n\le 10gN$ is a sum of at most $K(c)$ elements of $T$, repetition allowed.*

*Proof.* Set $C=16c^2$ and $u=n/g$. Since $g=C!$, every integer $j\in[1,C]$ divides $g$.

(a) *A popular sum.* The $|T|^2$ pairs in $T\times T$ have sums in $[1,4N]$, so some $\sigma\le 4N$ occurs as the sum of at least $|T|^2/(4N)$ pairs. Let $Y=\{x\in T:\sigma-x\in T\}$. Then $4N|Y|\ge |T|^2$, so $N^2\le c^2|T|^2\le 4c^2N|Y|$, which gives
$$N\le 4c^2|Y|.$$
In particular $Y$ is nonempty, and $Y\subseteq[1,\sigma-1]$, so $|Y|\le\sigma$.

(b) *Two translates meet.* Since $\sigma\le 4N\le C|Y|<(C+1)|Y|$, among the $(C+1)|Y|$ pairs $(i,x)$ with $0\le i\le C$ and $x\in Y$, two distinct pairs satisfy $x+iu\equiv x'+i'u\pmod\sigma$. If $i=i'$, then $x\equiv x'\pmod\sigma$ with $1\le x,x'<\sigma$, forcing $x=x'$, a contradiction. By symmetry assume $i<i'$ and put $j=i'-i\in[1,C]$. Then $x\equiv x'+ju\pmod\sigma$. Setting $z=\sigma-x'\in T$ gives
$$x+z\equiv ju\pmod\sigma,\qquad x\in Y,\quad z\in T.$$

(c) *Conclusion.* The integer $a=g/j$ satisfies $1\le a\le g$. We have $a(x+z)\equiv aju=n\pmod\sigma$ and $a(x+z)\le g\cdot 4N\le n$, so $n=a(x+z)+k\sigma$ for some integer $k\ge 0$. Because $x\in Y$, we can write $\sigma=x+(\sigma-x)$ with both summands in $T$. Thus $n$ is a sum of $2a+2k$ elements of $T$. Here $a\le g$, and
$$kN\le 4c^2k|Y|\le 4c^2k\sigma\le 4c^2n\le 40c^2gN,$$
so $k\le 40c^2g$. Therefore $2a+2k\le (2+80c^2)g=K(c)$. $\square$

## Lemma 6 (residues)

*Let $d\ge 1$.*

*(a) Every finite set $E_0\subseteq\mathbb N$ has a subset $E$ with $|E|<d$ and $s(E)\equiv s(E_0)\pmod d$.*

*(b) Suppose every integer $\ge m_0$ is a sum of distinct elements of $A$. Then for every $n\in\mathbb N$ there is a finite set $E\subseteq A$ with $|E|<d$, $s(E)\equiv n\pmod d$, and $s(E)\le d(m_0+1)$.*

*Proof.* (a) We induct on $|E_0|$. If $|E_0|<d$, take $E=E_0$. Otherwise list the elements of $E_0$ in any order as $x_1,\dots,x_l$ with $l\ge d$. Among the $l+1>d$ prefix sums $x_1+\dots+x_i$ ($0\le i\le l$), two are congruent modulo $d$, say for $i<i'$. Then $x_{i+1}+\dots+x_{i'}$ is divisible by $d$. Remove $x_{i+1},\dots,x_{i'}$ from $E_0$ and apply the induction hypothesis.

(b) Let $n_0$ be the remainder of $n$ modulo $d$, so $0\le n_0<d$. Since $n_0+dm_0\ge m_0$, there is a finite set $E_0\subseteq A$ with $s(E_0)=n_0+dm_0$. Let $E\subseteq E_0$ be as in part (a). Then $s(E)\equiv n_0\equiv n\pmod d$ and $s(E)\le s(E_0)<d+dm_0$. $\square$

## Lemma 7 (one scale)

*Let $N$ have type $c$ and set $g=g(c)$. If $g\mid n$ and $4gN\le n\le 10gN$, then $n\in D_{2hK(c),\,g}$.*

*Proof.* Apply Lemma 5 to $T=D_{2h,Q(c)}\cap[1,2N]$ to write $n$ as a sum of $m\le K(c)$ elements of $D_{2h,Q(c)}$. Since $g+2hm\le Q(c)$, Lemma 1(b) with $k=2h$ and $q=g$ gives $n\in D_{2hm,g}\subseteq D_{2hK(c),g}$. $\square$

## Lemma 8 (two consecutive scales)

*Suppose $N$ has type $c$ and $N+1$ has type $c'$, and set $g=g(c)$, $g'=g(c')$. If $g\mid n$ and $4gN\le n\le 5g'(N+1)$, then $n\in D_{2hK(c)+2hK(c'),\,g}$.*

*Proof.* If $n\le 10gN$, then $n\in D_{2hK(c),g}$ by Lemma 7, and monotonicity finishes the proof. Otherwise $10gN<n\le 5g'(N+1)\le 10g'N$, so $g<g'$ and hence $c<c'$.

Let $v$ be the largest element of $T=D_{2h,Q(c')}\cap[1,2(N+1)]$, which is nonempty because $N+1$ has type $c'$. Since $T\subseteq[1,v]$, we have $N+1\le c'|T|\le c'v$, and clearly $v\le 2(N+1)\le 4N$. Divide $n-4gN\ge 0$ by $gv$ with quotient $p\ge 0$ and remainder $\rho$:
$$n=n_2+pg\cdot v,\qquad n_2=4gN+\rho,\qquad 0\le\rho<gv\le 4gN.$$
Then $g\mid n_2$ (as $g\mid n$) and $4gN\le n_2\le 8gN$, so Lemma 7 gives $n_2\in D_{2hK(c),g}$. On the other hand, $pg\,v\le n\le 5g'(N+1)\le 5g'c'v$, so $pg\le 5c'g'\le K(c')$. Because $v\in D_{2h,Q(c')}$ and
$$\bigl(g+2hK(c)\bigr)+2h\cdot pg\le g'+2hK(c')+2hK(c')=Q(c'),$$
applying Lemma 1(b) to $pg$ copies of $v$ (with $k=2h$ and $q=g+2hK(c)$) and monotonicity gives $pg\cdot v\in D_{2hK(c'),\,g+2hK(c)}$. Finally, Lemma 1(a) gives $n=n_2+pg\cdot v\in D_{2hK(c)+2hK(c'),\,g}$. $\square$

## Proof of the theorem

Assume (i) and (ii). By Lemma 4 there is $N_1\ge 1$ such that every $N\ge N_1$ has some type at most $c_h$; pick one for each such $N$ and call it $\gamma(N)$. By (ii) there is $m_0$ such that every integer $\ge m_0$ is a sum of distinct elements of $A$. Set $N_2=N_1+m_0+1$, and consider any $n\ge 5\,g(\gamma(N_2))\,N_2$.

First, choose the scale. The inequality $5\,g(\gamma(N))\,N\le n$ holds at $N=N_2$ and fails for every $N>n$. Hence there is some $N\ge N_2$ for which it holds while failing at $N+1$. Put $c=\gamma(N)$, $c'=\gamma(N+1)$, $g=g(c)$, and $g'=g(c')$. Then
$$5gN\le n<5g'(N+1).$$

Next, fix the residue modulo $g$. By Lemma 6(b) with $d=g$, there exists $E\subseteq A$ with $|E|<g$, $s(E)\equiv n\pmod g$, and $s(E)\le g(m_0+1)\le gN$. Set $n_1=n-s(E)$. Then $g\mid n_1$ and $4gN\le n_1\le 5g'(N+1)$.

Finally, Lemma 8 gives $n_1\in D_{2hK(c)+2hK(c'),\,g}$. Since $s(E)\in D_{g,0}$, Lemma 1(a) shows that $n=s(E)+n_1\in D_{k,0}$ with
$$k=g(c)+2hK(c)+2hK(c')\le g(c_h)+4hK(c_h)=Q(c_h)=f(h).$$
Therefore $n$ is a sum of at most $f(h)$ distinct elements of $A$. $\square$

## What is new and what is borrowed

The question is 3(ii) in P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, *On bases with an exact order*, Acta Arith. 37 (1980), p. 206. Let $f^*(h)$ denote the smallest number that can play the role of $f(h)$ in the Theorem. The value $Q(c_h)$ proved here is only a huge upper bound on $f^*(h)$, not a serious estimate. N. Hegyvári, F. Hennecart, and A. Plagne (Combin. Probab. Comput. 16 (2007) 747-756) asked the question again and proved $f^*(h)\ge 2^{h-2}+h-1$ for $h\ge 3$. For $h=2$, the exact answer $f^*(2)=4$ was already known (Kelly 1957; Hennecart 2005).

### What is borrowed

Here [CYZ] denotes S.-Q. Chen, Q.-H. Yang, and L. Zhao, *On a problem of Erdős and Graham related to restricted order* (https://github.com/csq20180327/Erdos338, 18 Nov 2026, unrefereed).

* The overall proof plan comes from [CYZ]: counting pairs (Lemma 3), picking $r$ through a hierarchy of constants (Lemma 4), choosing disjoint representations greedily (Lemma 1), pigeonholing residues (Lemma 6), and fixing the residue first (proof of the Theorem).
* Earlier versions of this strategy, for sets of positive lower density, appear in D. Veljjanoski's note (https://github.com/veljjanoski/erdos338, 1 Oct 2026), which credits the disjoint-representation step to Hegyvári, Hennecart, and Plagne (2007).
* Iterating Lemma 2 recovers a theorem of Hegyvári, Hennecart, and Plagne (J. reine angew. Math. 560 (2003) 199-220, Theorem 4) in the form of Lemma 2 of [CYZ]: under (i), the sums of at most $h$ distinct elements of $A$ have positive lower density. We did not have access to the 2003 paper and did not compare proofs.
* Reducing a dense set modulo one integer and adding copies of it, as in Lemma 5, also appears (using Kneser's theorem) in the Lean formalization accompanying Veljjanoski's note.

### What is not proved here

[CYZ] proves that a basis has a restricted order if and only if sums of distinct elements hit every residue class modulo every $q$, and that this holds whenever $A$ minus any finite set remains a basis. They do not state a bound depending only on $h$.

### What appears to be new

After two incomplete literature searches up to 25 Nov 2026, the uniform bound depending only on $h$ appears to be new. Three choices make the uniformity work here: letting the number $Q(c)$ of forbidden elements depend on the scale's type $c$ and choosing it after the modulus $g(c)$, comparing two consecutive scales (Lemma 8), and using Lemma 5 in place of Kneser's theorem. A non-explicit bound also seems to follow from the proofs in [CYZ] via the full version of Kneser's theorem and a compactness argument (checked by hand only, not found in print), so a uniform bound should not be described as out of reach of their method. The header comment in `Erdos338.lean` lists further sources, credits, and limits of the searches.
